## Question 1

Let $X \sim N_p(\mu, \Sigma) \ with \ |\Sigma| > 0$. 

RTP:

$$
(X - \mu)'\Sigma^{-1}(X - \mu) \sim \chi^2_p 
$$

Using the eigen decomposition of $\Sigma$:  

$$
\Sigma = U\Lambda U^{'} 
$$
where $U$ is an orthogonal matrix, such that  
$$
U^{'} = U^{-1}
$$

Then
$$
\Sigma^{-1} = (U\Lambda U^{'})^{-1} 
= (U^{'})^{-1} \Lambda^{-1} U^{-1} 
= U\Lambda^{-1} U^{'} 
$$

Substituting in $\Sigma^{-1}$ 
$$
\begin{aligned}
(X - \mu)'\Sigma^{-1}(X - \mu)
&= (X - \mu)^{'} U\Lambda^{-1} U^{'}(X - \mu) \\
&= (X - \mu)^{'}U\Lambda^{-\frac{1}{2}} \Lambda^{-\frac{1}{2}} U^{'}(X - \mu)
\end{aligned}
$$

Let
$$
Y = \Lambda^{-\frac{1}{2}} U^{'}(X - \mu)
$$

and let
$$
A = \Lambda^{-\frac{1}{2}} U^{'}
$$

Therefore
$$
Y = A(X - \mu) \sim N_p(0, A\Sigma A^{'}) 
$$


Solve for the Covariance matrix of $Y$ 
$$
\begin{aligned}
A\Sigma A^{'}
&= (\Lambda^{-\frac{1}{2}} U^{'}) \ \Sigma \ (\Lambda^{-\frac{1}{2}} U^{'})^{'} \\
&= (\Lambda^{-\frac{1}{2}} U^{'}) \ \Sigma \ U(\Lambda^{-\frac{1}{2}} )^{'} \\
&= \Lambda^{-\frac{1}{2}} U^{'} \ U\Lambda U^{'} \ U(\Lambda^{-\frac{1}{2}})^{'} \\
&= \Lambda^{-\frac{1}{2}} \Lambda \ (\Lambda^{-\frac{1}{2}})^{'} \\
&= I_p
\end{aligned}
$$


$Y$ has a Multivariate Standard Normal Distribution.  
$$
Y \sim N_p(0, I_p)
$$

This means that individual $Y_i$ components have a Standard Normal Distribution. 
$$
Y_i \sim N(0, 1)
$$

The Sum of Squares of independent Standard Normal variables has a Chi-squared Distribution with $p$ degrees of freedom. 
$$
Y^{'}Y = \sum^{p}_{i = 1} Y^{2}_i
$$

$$
\sum^{p}_{i = 1} Y^{2}_i \sim \chi^{2}_p
$$


Since
$$
(X - \mu)'\Sigma^{-1}(X - \mu) = Y^{'}Y 
$$
We have that
$$
(X - \mu)'\Sigma^{-1}(X - \mu) \sim \chi^2_p
$$

## Question 2

$$
\mu = 
\begin{bmatrix}
5 \\
0 \\
-2\\
6 \\
2
\end{bmatrix}
$$

$$
\mu_{1} =
\begin{bmatrix}
5 \\
0 \\
6 
\end{bmatrix}
\quad
\mu_{2} = 
\begin{bmatrix}
-2 \\
2
\end{bmatrix}
$$

$$
\Sigma = 
\begin{bmatrix}
8 & 3 & 0 & -1 & 5 \\
3 & 12 & 2 & 2 & -2 \\
0 & 2 & 8 & 0 & 2 \\
-1 & 2 & 0 & 9 & 1 \\
5 & -2 & 2 & 1 & 10
\end{bmatrix}
$$

$$
\Sigma_{11} =
\begin{bmatrix}
8 & 3 & 0 \\
3 & 12 & 2 \\
0 & 2 & 8
\end{bmatrix}
\quad
\Sigma_{12} =
\begin{bmatrix}
-1 & 5 \\
2 & -2 \\
0 & 2
\end{bmatrix}
\quad
\Sigma_{21} =
\begin{bmatrix}
-1 & 2 & 0 \\
5 & -2 & 2 
\end{bmatrix}
\quad
\Sigma_{22} =
\begin{bmatrix}
9 & 1 \\
1 & 10 
\end{bmatrix}
$$
$\mu_{1 \mid 2} = \mu_{1} + \Sigma_{12}\Sigma_{22}^{-1}(x_{2} - \mu_{2})$

$x_{2} - \mu_{2}$:
$$
x_{2} - \mu_{2} = 
\begin{bmatrix}
-1 \\
2
\end{bmatrix}
\quad
-
\quad
\begin{bmatrix}
-2 \\
2
\end{bmatrix}
\quad
=
\quad
\begin{bmatrix}
1 \\
0
\end{bmatrix}
\quad
$$

$$
\Sigma_{22}^{-1} = 
\begin{bmatrix}
\frac{10}{89} & \frac{-1}{89} \\
\frac{-1}{89} & \frac{9}{89} 
\end{bmatrix}
$$
Now that we have values for all the parameters, $\mu_{1 \mid 2}$ can easily be computed to give us:
$$
\mu_{1 \mid 2} = 
\begin{bmatrix}
\frac{430}{89}\\
\frac{22}{89} \\
\frac{-2}{89}
\end{bmatrix}
$$

$\Sigma_{1 \mid 2} = \Sigma_{11} - \Sigma_{12}\Sigma_{22}^{-1}\Sigma_{21}$

Resulting in a 3x3 matrix:
$$
\Sigma_{1 \mid 2} =
\begin{bmatrix}
-237 & 125 & -92 \\
125 & -72 & 42 \\
-92 & 42 & -28
\end{bmatrix}
$$
$$
X_{1}\mid X_{2} =
\begin{bmatrix}
-1 \\
2
\end{bmatrix}
\sim
N_{3}(\mu_{1 \mid 2}, \Sigma_{1 \mid 2})
$$

Giving us a final answer of:

$$
X_{1}\mid X_{2} =
\begin{bmatrix}
-1 \\
2
\end{bmatrix}
\sim
N_{3}
(
\begin{bmatrix}
\frac{430}{89}\\
\frac{22}{89} \\
\frac{-2}{89}
\end{bmatrix}
,
\quad
\begin{bmatrix}
-237 & 125 & -92 \\
125 & -72 & 42 \\
-92 & 42 & -28
\end{bmatrix}
)
$$
